instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If my opponent has a card that says all damage from creatures is prevented, can I still use a creature's special ability to deal damage?

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if my creature is attacking, but my opponent prevents all combat damage and I have an effect that doubles all damage dealt by my creatures?

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if my enchantment is destroyed but the effect says it should endure 2?
output: When an enchantment is instructed to endure 2, you have a choice to ensure its presence remains on the battlefield. You can either create a 2/2 white Spirit creature token or put two +1/+1 counters on that permanent. For example, if your enchantment is destroyed but told to endure 2, you could choose to create a 2/2 white Spirit token instead of the enchantment simply going to the graveyard.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I mulligan my starting hand in a multiplayer game without having to reduce my hand size?
output: Yes, you can. In a multiplayer game, the first mulligan a player takes does not count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take. For example, if you are playing in a four-player game and draw seven cards but want to try again, you can mulligan and still receive a full hand of seven cards.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I use an ability to create a token? Does it get all the same powers as my card?
output: When you use an ability to create a token, the game defines the token based only on what that specific ability says. The spell or ability that creates a token may define the values of any number of characteristics, and those become the token's text. A token has no characteristics not defined by the spell or ability that created it. For example, if you use Jade Mage to create a 1/1 green Saproling creature token, that Saproling will have no rules text or abilities because the ability did not define them.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a Vesuvan Doppelganger that is already copying another creature?
output: First, the Clone enters as a copy of the Doppelganger. Because the copy's copiable values become the copied information, the Clone then adopts the characteristics the Doppelganger has already taken from its target. For example, if a Vesuvan Doppelganger is currently copying a 2/2 green Bear, the Clone will enter the battlefield as a 2/2 blue Bear named after that Bear and will also have the Doppelganger's upkeep ability to become a copy of another creature.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I just played this Vehicle card, but it's not a creature yet. Can I attack with it right away?
output: No, you cannot attack with it while it is only an artifact. A Vehicle has its printed power and toughness only if it is also a creature. You must use the crew ability to turn it into an artifact creature before it can participate in combat. For example, if you play a Vehicle with crew 2, you need to tap two other creatures to make it a creature so that it can attack.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I still use a card's Scavenge ability if it is sitting in my graveyard instead of being on the battlefield?
output: Yes, you can. Scavenge is an activated ability that functions only while the card with scavenge is in a graveyard. For example, if you have a creature with 3 power that has Scavenge in your graveyard, you can pay its cost and exile it to put three +1/+1 counters on another creature you control.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I just played an equipment with living weapon. What actually happens to the board?
output: When you cast an equipment with living weapon, a sequence of events occurs. First, the ability triggers because the equipment is entering the battlefield. This triggers the effect to create a 0/0 black Phyrexian Germ creature token, then attach this equipment to it. For example, if you cast Batterskull, you will first see a 0/0 black Phyrexian Germ token appear, and then Batterskull will immediately attach itself to that Germ, making it a 4/4 creature.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I use the text in the middle of the card to identify what it is called?
output: No, you cannot because the name of a card is printed on its upper left corner. For example, if a card has an ability that says This creature is a Dragon, you must still look at the top left corner to find the actual name of the card.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to the way we pass packs when we move from the first round to the second round of drafting?
output: The direction of passing changes for the middle round. In the first and third draft rounds, booster packs are passed to each player's left, but in the second draft round, they are passed to each player's right. For example, if you were passing your pack to the person on your left during the first round, you will instead pass it to the person on your right when the second round starts.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I cast an enchantment that targets a creature, but my opponent destroys that creature before the enchantment actually resolves?
output: The enchantment will not enter the battlefield. When a spell resolves, it checks whether its target is still legal. If the target is no longer legal, the spell does not resolve and is instead removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast an enchantment like Aura of Luminous Ambition targeting an opponent's creature, but they use a spell like Murder to destroy that creature in response, your enchantment will fail to resolve and go directly to your graveyard.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when my opponent destroys the land I just earthbent?
output: When that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control. For example, if you use an effect to earthbend a Plains and your opponent plays a spell to destroy all creatures, your Plains will be put into the graveyard but will immediately come back to the battlefield tapped.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I'm the monarch right now, but my opponent just played a card that makes them the monarch too. Do we both get to draw an extra card at the start of our turns?
output: No, you will not both draw the extra card. Only one player can be the monarch at a time, and as a player becomes the monarch, the current monarch ceases to be the monarch. For example, if you are currently the monarch and your opponent plays a spell that makes them the monarch, your status ends immediately when that spell resolves, meaning only they will draw the extra card at the start of their turn.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I use two different cards that both say they add an extra combat phase right after my main phase?
output: When you use effects that add phases, they are added directly after the specified phase. If multiple extra phases are created after the same phase, the most recently created phase will occur first. For example, if you cast a spell that adds a combat phase after your main phase and then cast another spell that also adds a combat phase after your main phase, the combat phase from the second spell will happen before the combat phase from the first spell.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: My opponent just played a card that destroys all permanents. Does my emblem get destroyed too?
output: No, your emblem stays on the field. When the spell resolves, it looks for permanents to destroy, but because an emblem is neither a card nor a permanent, it is not affected by the effect. For example, if you have an emblem and your opponent casts a spell like Wrath of God that destroys all creatures, your emblem remains because it is not a permanent.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to my creatures when I play an enchantment that says they all get flying?
output: The creatures gain the flying ability because an ability can be defined by an object's rules text or by the effect that created it. When the enchantment resolves, the effect modifies the creatures to include that new characteristic. For example, if you have a 1/1 creature with no abilities and play an enchantment that grants flying, that creature now has the flying ability.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I have an enchantment that forces me to attack and another effect that makes my creatures unblockable?
output: The game applies effects that change game rules, such as a requirement to attack, after all other continuous effects have been applied. This means the game first determines the state of your creatures, such as them being unblockable, and then applies the rule that you must attack. For example, if you have an effect making your creatures unblockable and an enchantment like Archon of Coronation forcing an attack, the game first processes the unblockable status before applying the mandatory attack requirement.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I have an effect that turns my artifacts into 2/2 creatures, and then another effect that gives them +1/+1? Do they both work even though they weren't creatures to begin with?
output: When multiple effects apply to an object in different stages, the game applies the parts of the effect in their appropriate ones. If an effect starts to apply in one stage, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable stage, even if those objects change. For example, an effect that makes all noncreature artifacts 2/2 artifact creatures is both a type-changing effect and a power-and-toughness-setting effect. The game first turns them into creatures and then applies the 2/2 power and toughness to those same objects.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I play a creature while my opponent has a Space Sculptor on the field?
output: When a permanent with space sculptor and creatures without a sector designation are on the battlefield at the same time, players choose a sector designation for those creatures. For example, if your opponent controls a Space Sculptor and you cast a creature, that creature enters without a designation. Because these conditions are met, you will get to choose whether that creature is in the alpha, beta, or gamma sector.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I still use the adventure part of an adventurer card if it is sitting in my graveyard?
output: No, you cannot. In every zone except the stack, an adventurer card has only its normal characteristics. This means that while the card is in your graveyard, it does not function as an adventure spell. For example, if Brazen Borrower is in your graveyard, you cannot cast its adventure portion because the card only possesses its normal characteristics in that zone.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to a creature when I use a spell to make a copy of another creature spell?
output: When the copy of a permanent spell resolves, it becomes a token. This is because a copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves and has the characteristics of the spell that became that token. For example, if you use a spell to copy a creature spell that is a 2/2 Red Goblin, the resulting token will be a 2/2 Red Goblin.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I exile a card? Does my opponent get to see what it is?
output: By default, any card you exile is kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. For example, if you use a spell to exile a creature from your graveyard, that card stays face up so everyone can see its name and abilities.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have four copies of Lightning Bolt in my main deck, can I put one of them in my sideboard to swap it out later?
output: No, you cannot do that. In constructed play, the four-card limit applies to the combined deck and sideboard. Since you already have four copies of the card in your main deck, you cannot add any additional copies to your sideboard. For example, if you have four copies of Counterspell in your main deck, you are not allowed to have a fifth copy in your sideboard.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when a card says I get an emblem with a special power?
output: When you receive an emblem, you put that emblem into your command zone. This is because the rules state that the player gets an emblem that is both owned and controlled by them. For example, if a spell says you get an emblem with all your creatures gaining flying, you place that emblem in your command zone to begin using that ability.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if a spell says the player with the most life wins, but two people are tied at exactly 20 life?
output: There is no automatic way for the game to decide who wins in that situation. If an effect could result in a tie, the text of the spell or ability that created the effect will specify what to do in the event of a tie. Because the Magic game has no default for ties, you cannot assume the person who reached that life total first or the active player is the winner unless the card explicitly says so. For example, if a card simply says 'the player with the most life wins' and two players both have 20 life, the game does not have a built-in rule to break that tie.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: My commander just got exiled by an opponent's spell. Can I get him back into my command zone right away?
output: Yes, you can move your commander back to the command zone. In a Commander game, if a commander is in exile and it was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. For example, if an opponent casts a spell that exiles your commander, you can take that commander from exile and place it back in your command zone during the next check.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: We chose the limited range of influence option, but this plane effect says everyone gets a bonus. Does it really hit every player?
output: Yes, it does. Plane cards and phenomenon cards are exempt from the limited range of influence option, meaning their abilities affect all applicable objects and players in the game. For example, if a plane card says each player draws a card, every player at the table will draw a card even though you have chosen to limit the range of influence for other effects.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if someone uses an effect to restart the game while we are playing with limited influence? Does everyone have to start over or just the people that player was interacting with?
output: Everyone in the game is involved in the restart. Even if the person who controls the ability that restarts the game only has a limited range of influence, all players in the game are involved. For example, if four players are playing and Player A's abilities only affect Player B, but Player A then uses an effect to restart the game, Players C and D must also participate in the restart.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I see a card that says Plane — Serra's Realm? Does it have two subtypes?
output: You treat the entire phrase after the dash as one unit. Because all words after the dash are, collectively, a single subtype, you do not count them as separate types. For example, on a card labeled Plane — Serra's Realm, you identify the entire phrase Serra's Realm as its one and only subtype.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I have three Demons on the battlefield and one face-down Demon, but my win condition requires me to control four Demons with different names?
output: The win condition does not trigger. Because the group of creatures includes one with no name, those creatures do not count as having different names. To satisfy such a requirement, every object must have at least one name and no two objects can share a name. For example, if you control a Demon named Rakdos, a Demon named Belial, and a nameless face-down Demon, you only have two Demons with different names.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if we are playing a little side game for a bonus and that game gets restarted?
output: When a subgame is restarted, the main game remains unaffected, but any effects in the main game that refer to the winner or loser of the subgame will now refer to the winner or loser of the restarted subgame. For example, if you have an enchantment that says You gain 3 life if the winner of the side game has more creatures than you, and the side game restarts, that effect will now trigger based on whoever wins the new side game.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if my creature hits a planeswalker for 3 damage?
output: When you deal damage to a planeswalker, that many loyalty counters are removed from it. For example, if you attack with a 3/3 creature and choose the planeswalker as the target for combat damage, you will remove 3 loyalty counters from that planeswalker.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I am about to lose the game because my life hits zero and I also run out of cards in my library at the same time, but I have a card that says instead of losing, I shuffle and draw seven?
output: You will not lose. When state-based actions are checked, the game identifies all reasons you would lose at that moment. Because if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them, your card handles all those losses with one effect. For example, if you have Lich's Mirror and an event causes you to hit zero life and run out of cards in your library simultaneously, the mirror replaces that loss with its shuffle-and-draw effect.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I still use the abilities on my scheme card if it is sitting in the command zone instead of being played?
output: Yes, you can. The mechanic is that any abilities of a face-up scheme card in the command zone function from that zone. This means its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated. For example, if your scheme card has a static ability that says all creatures you control get plus one plus one, that bonus still applies to your creatures even while the card is in the command zone.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: My teammate and I can't decide which of our creatures should attack. Who gets to make the final choice?
output: If you and your teammate cannot agree on a choice, such as which creatures attack, the responsibility falls to a designated primary player. This person is defined as the player seated in the rightmost seat from that team's perspective. For example, if you are playing on a two-person team and you and your partner disagree on whether to attack with a 2/2 creature or a 3/3 creature, the person sitting furthest to the right from your team's point of view decides.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: My friend and I are playing Two-Headed Giant, but he is sitting all the way on the other side of the table from me. Can we still take our turns together as one team?
output: No, you cannot use shared team turns in that arrangement. Shared team turns can be used only if the members of each team are sitting in adjacent seats. For example, if you are playing Two-Headed Giant but your teammate is sitting directly across from you instead of right next to you, you must take separate turns rather than sharing a single team turn.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I use an ability to boost a Vehicle's power while it is still just an artifact?
output: The effect is created even though it does not do anything until the permanent becomes a creature. Because a noncreature permanent has no power or toughness, even if it has numbers printed on it, the modification is applied to the object so that it is ready once the Vehicle is crewed. For example, if you cast a spell to give an uncrewed Skysovereign, Intervention Supreme +2/+2, the bonus will be waiting and apply as soon as you crew the Vehicle and it becomes a creature.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to my planeswalker's loyalty when I use an ability that costs minus 2 loyalty?
output: When you activate such an ability, you are removing loyalty counters from the card. Because a planeswalker's loyalty on the battlefield is equal to the number of loyalty counters on it, the loyalty value changes to match the new counter count. For example, if your planeswalker has 5 loyalty and you use an ability that costs minus 2 loyalty, the card will then have 3 loyalty counters on it, meaning its loyalty is now 3.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to my Sagas when I reach my first main phase?
output: During your precombat main phase, you put a lore counter on each Saga you control that has one or more chapter abilities. This is an automatic turn-based action. For example, if you have The Eldest Reborn on the battlefield, you will add its first lore counter as soon as you enter your precombat main phase.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I sacrifice a creature to pay for the casualty cost on my spell?
output: When you cast a spell with casualty and pay that cost, the rule states that you copy the spell and, if the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for the copy. For example, if you cast a spell with Casualty 3 that targets an opponent's creature, and you sacrifice a 3-power creature to pay the cost, you will have both the original spell and a copy of it on the stack, allowing you to pick a different target for the copy.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I try to use a Treasure token to get some mana?
output: To use a Treasure token for mana, you follow its specific instructions. A Treasure token is a colorless Treasure artifact token with {T}, Sacrifice this token: Add one mana of any color. This means you tap the token and sacrifice it to move it to your graveyard, which then allows you to add one mana of any color you choose to your mana pool. For example, if you have a Treasure token and need to cast a green spell, you tap the token, sacrifice it, and add {G}.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I cast a creature with Squad 2 and decide to pay 6 mana for the squad cost instead of just 2?
output: You will end up with four creatures total: the original creature you cast and three token copies. This is because paying a squad cost is an additional cost that you may pay any number of times when casting the spell, and when the creature enters, if its squad cost was paid, you create a token that is a copy of it for each time its squad cost was paid. For example, by paying 6 mana for a Squad 2 ability, you have effectively paid the cost three times, which results in the original creature plus three tokens.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If I use an effect that converts a creature to its other face, will it trigger my opponent's ability that says 'Whenever a permanent is turned face down, draw a card'?
output: No, it will not trigger. Although converting uses the same physical action of turning a card over, they are different game actions. Abilities that trigger when a permanent is turned face down won't trigger when that permanent converts. For example, if your opponent has an enchantment that triggers whenever a creature is turned face down, and you use an effect to convert one of their creatures directly to its other face, that enchantment will not trigger.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: We decided to add a rule where everyone draws an extra card and another rule where creatures get bigger when they attack. What happens if we try to use both at the same time?
output: Both rules will be active in your game. This is because the rules consist of a series of options that can be added to a multiplayer game, meaning you can layer multiple additions on top of each other. For example, during your turn, you would first draw your extra card and then move to combat where your creatures receive their size bonus. You can use as many options as you like, but you must ensure you are only using one variant style of play.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if my opponent casts a spell and it finishes resolving? Can I play something now, or do they get to go again?
output: After a spell or ability resolves, the active player receives priority. This means if your opponent is currently taking their turn and a spell they cast finishes resolving, they get the first chance to take an action before you can respond with your own spell. For example, if your opponent casts a spell that draws them a card and it resolves, they receive priority immediately after, which might allow them to cast another spell before you have the opportunity to play anything.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I flip over a phenomenon card from my planar deck?
output: When you move a phenomenon card off a planar deck and turn it face up, you encounter it, which triggers that card's ability. For example, if you have a phenomenon card titled Great Flood that says When you encounter Great Flood, destroy target creature, the destruction effect happens as soon as you flip the card from the deck and turn it face up.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I search for a land that is an Island if my spell says I need to find a basic land?
output: You can only do so if that Island also has the supertype basic. Any land that does not have the supertype basic is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type. For example, if you use a spell to search for a basic land and you only have an Island that lacks the supertype basic, you cannot select that land.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I tap three lands for three mana but only spend two to cast a spell?
output: When an effect instructs a player to add mana, that mana goes into your mana pool and it can be used to pay costs immediately or stay in your mana pool as unspent mana. This mana will remain available until the end of the current step and phase. For example, if you tap three lands to add three blue mana during your main phase and only use two to cast a spell, you can keep that remaining one blue mana to cast another spell later in that same main phase.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: My friend says my deck is illegal because of some tournament rules, but I don't see those rules anywhere in this book. What happens when there's a disagreement like this?
output: A disagreement like this occurs because many multiplayer Magic tournaments have additional rules not included here, including rules for deck construction. To resolve the conflict, you would need to check the most current Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules at WPN.wizards.com/en/rules-documents to find the specific requirements for your event. For example, if you bring a deck with 100 cards and the tournament organizers have added a rule that all decks must be exactly 60 cards, the judge will use those additional rules to declare your deck illegal.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I use Magar of the Magic Strings to copy a creature that had its power increased by an effect right before it died?
output: First, you note the name of the card in the graveyard. Then, you create the copy by using the characteristics of that card as it last existed in the graveyard to determine the copiable values. This ensures any modifications are included. For example, if a 2/2 creature had its power increased to 4 right before being put into the graveyard, your copy will be a 4-power creature.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I cast a creature using its Blitz cost? Does it stay on the battlefield permanently?
output: When you pay the blitz cost, the creature enters the battlefield with haste and a card-draw ability. However, because you paid that specific cost, a delayed trigger will occur where you must sacrifice the permanent at the beginning of the next end step. For example, if you cast a creature using its blitz cost during your turn, it will stay on the battlefield through your combat phase, but you will be forced to sacrifice it once the next end step begins.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have a card with Transfigure on it. If I decide to use that ability, what exactly does it do?
output: When you use Transfigure, you must pay the required cost and sacrifice the permanent you are using. Then, you search your library for a creature card that has the same mana value as the one you just sacrificed and put it onto the battlefield. Finally, you shuffle your library. For example, if you have a 2-mana creature with Transfigure and you activate it, you sacrifice that creature and then search your deck for any other creature that costs 2 mana to put into play.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I just pulled this new card and it has these weird lines in the text area and some icons. Is there a specific way to tell if it is one of those station cards?
output: You can identify them by looking for a few specific features. Each station card has a striated text box and will contain one or two station symbols within that text box. For example, if you play a card called Frontier Outpost that has a striped-looking text area and a single station symbol, you know it functions as a station card.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to my spells after they finish working?
output: After an instant or sorcery spell finishes resolving, it moves from the stack to your graveyard. The rules specify that any instant or sorcery spell that has finished resolving is put on top of its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast a Fireball and the damage is dealt, the card moves from the stack into your discard pile.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I cast this card from my graveyard by just tapping a creature instead of paying its mana cost?
output: It depends on the specific harmonize cost. If a card has a harmonize cost, you may cast it from your graveyard by paying that cost and tapping an untapped creature you control instead of paying the spell's normal mana cost. However, you do not just tap a creature; you also pay the mana specified in the harmonize cost, which is then reduced by the tapped creature's power. For example, if a card has a harmonize cost of 2, and you tap a 2/2 creature, your total cost for the spell would be 0 generic mana rather than 2.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I am playing a card that affects all creatures with a certain name, but my version looks different. Does the effect still work on my creature?
output: Yes, it does. For the purposes of all rules, abilities, and effects that refer to a card name, objects with interchangeable names have the same name. For example, if an ability targets every creature named Silver Dragon and you play a version of Silver Dragon that has an interchangeable names indicator, the effect will treat it as having that name.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if a card says something is supposed to happen right when my turn ends? Can I use a spell to stop it?
output: It depends on whether the effect is a turn-based action or a triggered ability. Turn-based actions happen automatically when steps or phases begin or end and do not use the stack. However, most cards use triggered abilities, such as an enchantment that says At the beginning of your end step, sacrifice this artifact. Because this ability watches for a phase to begin, it is a triggered ability that goes on the stack, meaning you can use spells to respond to it.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when a card says my life becomes 5, but I already have 12 life?
output: You lose 7 life. When an effect sets your life total to a specific number, you lose the necessary amount of life to end up with that new total. For example, if you have 12 life and a card says your life becomes 5, you lose 7 life so that your life total ends at exactly 5.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have a card in my graveyard that says Aftermath on it. Can I actually play it from there?
output: Yes, you can. The Aftermath ability means you may cast this half of this split card from your graveyard. For example, if you have a spell with Aftermath in your graveyard, you can pay its mana cost to cast it directly from the graveyard rather than needing to draw it into your hand first.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I just played a card that says it has Daybound, but it's night in our game. Does it stay as the front side or does it flip over right away?
output: It flips over immediately. The Daybound ability states that if it is night and the permanent is represented by a double-faced card, it enters transformed. For example, if you cast a creature with Daybound while it is currently night, it will enter the battlefield already transformed into its back face.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If I don't want to play any cards or attack, do I still have to go through all those different parts of the turn?
output: Yes, you must go through every stage. The rules specify that each of the five phases—beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, and ending—takes place every turn, even if nothing happens during the phase. For example, if you have no lands to play and no spells in hand, you still move from the beginning phase through the precombat main phase before your turn officially ends.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If I use the monstrosity ability on my creature, can I use it again later in the game?
output: No, you cannot. The rule states that if this permanent isn't monstrous, you put N +1/+1 counters on it and it becomes monstrous. Once a permanent becomes monstrous, it stays monstrous until it leaves the battlefield. For example, if you have a creature with Monstrosity 3 and you activate its ability, it gets three +1/+1 counters and is now monstrous. You won't be able to trigger that ability again even if you have extra mana because the creature is already monstrous.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to my teammate when I play a card that gives me an extra turn in Two-Headed Giant?
output: Your teammate will also take that extra turn. Because you are on the same team, any effect that gives a player an extra turn or adds a phase or step to that player's turn means that player's team takes the extra turn. For example, if you cast a spell in Two-Headed Giant that says you take an extra turn, your teammate will proceed through that extra turn along with you.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to my cards and the current plane if I have to leave the game?
output: When you leave the game, all objects you own, including your lands and creatures, leave the game. If this process includes leaving a face-up plane card, the planar controller must turn the top card of their planar deck face up. For example, if you are playing on a plane called Zendikar and you leave the match, your entire board state is removed from play, and the next plane in the deck is flipped over to become the new active plane.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: My opponent just played a card that says I skip my next turn. Can I still cast spells and tap lands during the rest of my current turn?
output: Yes, you can. Once a step, phase, or turn has already started, it can no longer be skipped. Any effect that causes you to skip your next turn will wait until the next occurrence of a turn. For example, if your opponent casts a spell to skip your next turn while you are currently in your combat phase, you will finish your current combat phase and the rest of your current turn as normal. The skip effect will only take effect when your next actual turn begins.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I finish my mulligans and realize I have a card that should be on the battlefield immediately?
output: Once the mulligan process is complete, you may take any such actions in any order. If the card allows you to begin the game with it on the battlefield, you put that card onto the battlefield. The starting player performs these actions first, and then each other player follows in turn order. For example, if you are the starting player, you would place your special permanent on the table right after your mulligans are done but before your first turn begins.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens when I play a card that tempts the Ring but I don't have an emblem yet?
output: If you do not have an emblem named The Ring at the time the Ring tempts you, you get an emblem named The Ring before choosing a creature to be your Ring-bearer. For example, if you cast a spell that causes the Ring to tempt you for the first time, you will immediately gain The Ring emblem and then select one of your creatures, such as a 2/2 Goblin, to become your Ring-bearer.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I try to use a spell to move an Aura from my creature onto a Land?
output: Nothing happens. If an effect tries to attach an Aura to an object it cannot enchant, the Aura does not move. For example, if you have an Aura like Rancor attached to a creature and you use a spell that says attach target Aura to target land, the Rancor stays on the creature because it cannot be attached to an object it could not enchant.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I want to use a battle card from my hand during my turn?
output: You can cast the battle card as a spell during your main phase as long as the stack is empty. For example, once you have finished playing your lands and other spells and there are no more actions waiting to resolve, you can cast the battle card which then goes on the stack for players to respond to.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I build a deck with 150 cards for a regular tournament?
output: Yes, you can. This is because while formats have a minimum deck size that must be met, there is no maximum deck size for non-Commander decks. For example, if you are playing Modern and must have at least 60 cards, you could legally build a deck with 150 cards.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have a creature with no abilities, and I have a card out that gives +2/+2 to creatures with no abilities. If I use an enchantment to give that creature flying, does it still get the +2/+2 bonus?
output: No, the creature will no longer get the +2/+2 bonus. When you use an enchantment to give a creature flying, you are granting it an ability. The rule clarifies that an effect that grants an ability is different from an effect that simply states a quality of an object. Once the creature has the flying ability, it no longer meets the requirement of having no abilities. For example, if you enchant a Runeclaw Bear with an Aura that gives it flying, it will not get the +2/+2 bonus from Muraganda Petroglyphs.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If my opponent plays a spell that destroys all artifacts, can they destroy the ones in my sideboard?
output: No, they cannot. This is because cards in a player's sideboard are outside the game, and cards outside the game cannot be affected by spells or abilities. For example, if your opponent plays a spell that destroys all artifacts, none of the artifacts you have sitting in your sideboard will be destroyed because they are not in any of the game's zones.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Why does the player playing the archenemy have so much more health than us? We only started with 20.
output: In this game format, the archenemy's starting life total is 40 and each other player's starting life total is 20. For example, if you and your teammate are playing against one opponent, you both begin with 20 life while that single opponent starts with 40 life.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens to the owner of a scheme card once it is turned face up?
output: Ownership shifts to whoever is currently controlling the card. While the player who started with the card in their command zone is typically the owner, once it is flipped face up, ownership is determined by who controls it. For example, if Player A has a scheme card in their command zone and it is flipped face up, they own it, but if Player B takes control of that face-up card, Player B becomes the owner because the controller of a face-up scheme card is its owner.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if it is day and my opponent goes through their whole turn without casting anything?
output: The time of day will change to night. If it is day and the previous turn's active player didn't cast any spells during that turn, it becomes night. For example, if your opponent passes their turn without playing any cards while it is daytime, the game will transition to night.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Wait, since we have extra people playing on each side now, do we change how far apart everyone sits?
output: Yes, you must adjust the range of influence if the teams have more than three players. A general's range should be the minimum number that allows one opposing general to begin the game within their range, and an emperor's range should be the minimum number that allows two generals from opposing teams to begin within their range. For example, in a game with two teams of four players, the emperor has a range of 3, the second general (General 2) has a range of 2, and the first and third generals have a range of 1.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have a creature with 3/1 on it. If my opponent attacks me with a 2/2, will my creature survive?
output: No, your creature will be destroyed. The second number on the card is its toughness, which is the amount of damage needed to destroy it. Since your creature only has 1 toughness and the attacking creature deals 2 damage, it will not survive. For example, if you had a 3/3 creature instead, it would survive because 2 damage is less than its toughness of 3.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If I am forced to discard a card with Madness, do I just put it in the graveyard or can I do something else?
output: Instead of putting the card into your graveyard, you exile it instead. When this card is exiled this way, its owner may cast it by paying the madness cost rather than its mana cost. If you choose not to cast it, you put the card into your graveyard. For example, if you have a card with Madness 3 in hand and an effect forces you to discard it, you exile that card and can then pay 3 mana to cast it immediately.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if I hit my opponent with a creature that has toxic 2?
output: When combat damage is dealt to a player by a creature with toxic, you give that player a number of poison counters equal to the creature's total toxic value, in addition to the damage. For example, if your creature with toxic 2 deals 3 damage to an opponent, they will receive 2 poison counters.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have a card that makes tokens and another that untaps my creatures whenever a token enters, and it's going to take forever. Can I just tell everyone I'm going to do this a thousand times so we don't have to go through every single step?
output: Yes, you can suggest a shortcut by describing a sequence of game choices that may be legally taken based on the current game state. This sequence can include a loop that repeats a specified number of times. For example, if you control a creature that creates a 1/1 token when tapped and an artifact that untaps all creatures whenever a creature enters, you can suggest a shortcut by saying you will repeat the sequence of tapping the creature, letting the token ability resolve, and letting the untap ability resolve 999,999 more times. Each other player then has a chance to either accept your proposal or name a point where they would make a different game choice. If everyone accepts, the game advances to the end of that sequence.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: What happens if we need to decide who starts the game?
output: You must randomly determine which emperor goes first, and then the turn order goes to the players' left. For example, if you flip a coin and it lands on heads for Player A, the person sitting to their left will be the next one to take a turn.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: Can I still say I attacked you if my creature gets destroyed before it hits you?
output: Yes, you can, because a player has attacked if they declare one or more creatures as attackers attacking the second player. For example, if you declare a 2/2 creature as an attacker but your opponent uses a spell to destroy it before it deals damage, you still technically attacked them during that combat phase.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: If I am casting a spell that costs two mana and also requires me to sacrifice a creature, but I have a card on the table that makes my spells cheaper, do I calculate the discount before or after the sacrifice?
output: You calculate everything together before you pay anything. When casting a spell, you first propose the spell and then determine the total cost. This process involves taking the mana cost, adding any additional costs like a sacrifice, and subtracting any cost reductions. Once this calculation is finished, the resulting total cost becomes locked in. For example, if you are casting Altar's Reap which costs {1}{B} and has an additional cost of sacrificing a creature, and you have Thunderscape Familiar on the battlefield that makes your black spells cost {1} less, you determine the total cost as {B} plus the sacrifice. After that, the cost is locked in, and then you proceed to pay it.

instruction: You are an MTG expert. Answer this question.
input: I have a creature with Support 2 on the field. Can I use its ability to put a counter on itself and another creature?
output: No, you cannot. When Support N is on a permanent, it means you put a +1/+1 counter on each of up to N other target creatures. Because the rule specifies other target creatures, the creature providing the support cannot be one of the targets. For example, if you have a 2/2 creature with Support 2, you can choose two other creatures to receive counters, but you cannot choose that same 2/2 creature as one of your targets.
